text: On-orbit servicing is not science fiction: astronauts visited Hubble five times between 1993 and 2009 to repair and upgrade it.
To move from one circular orbit to another with the least fuel you use a Hohmann transfer: one burn to enter an ellipse and another to circularize.
source: Hohmann transfer; NASA, Basics of Space Flight (JPL)

text: Every m/s costs propellant. The Tsiolkovsky equation tells you how much: Δv = Isp · g0 · ln(m0/mf).
source: Tsiolkovsky rocket equation; NASA Glenn, Beginner's Guide to Rockets

text: On Servicing Mission 4 (2009) the Atlantis crew performed five spacewalks on Hubble.
A satellite in low orbit passes over a ground station for a few minutes per orbit. Outside that window there is no link.
source: NASA, CubeSat 101: Basic Concepts and Processes for First-Time CubeSat Developers

text: Loss of signal (LOS): the station has dropped below the horizon. The work waits for the next pass.
Overshot? A negative burn lowers the orbit with the same Hohmann logic.
Mass rules: everything you take up has to be pushed. That is why every mission has a mass budget.
source: NASA, Design and Develop Science Missions (space segment)

text: Servicing mission complete. Hubble is still operating decades after its 1990 launch thanks to those repairs.
Missions are designed by segments: launch, space, ground and user. This level goes through all of them.
source: NASA, Design and Develop Science Missions

text: A sun-synchronous orbit passes over each latitude at the same local solar time: ideal for comparing images from different days.
source: NASA Earth Observatory, Catalog of Earth Satellite Orbits

text: Inclination limits the latitudes you can see: at 0° you only cover the equatorial band.
source: NASA Earth Observatory, Catalog of Earth Satellite Orbits

text: Data that does not fit in memory is lost. The downlink matters as much as the instrument.
In low orbit, about a third of each orbit can be in eclipse: the battery keeps the spacecraft alive in Earth's shadow.
source: Eclipse geometry in a circular orbit

text: Ikaros is based on the power system design of Solar Probe+, the mission that flew as Parker Solar Probe.
source: Landis et al., AIAA 2008-5712; NASA, Parker Solar Probe

text: ⚗ The reactor, the HTS field, the nanobots and the return capsule are theoretical extensions of the game, not NASA data.
Solar Probe+ is a mass-limited mission: it needs a very high launch C3.
Each Venus flyby slows the spacecraft relative to the Sun and lowers the perihelion. The real design uses 7; here there are 3.
Parker Solar Probe made its seventh and final Venus flyby in November 2024.
At 0.25 AU sunlight is 16 times stronger than at Earth. The main array is no longer usable and folds behind the shield.
From here on only the secondary array works: ~1 cm² concentrator cells with a coolant loop.
Tilting the array reduces the light it receives: the paper goes up to ~74° to keep it below 180 °C.
The cells operate at 120 °C. Heat that is not turned into electricity is rejected by radiators at 100 °C.
Above ~350 °C the cells degrade permanently.
The spacecraft needs at least 482 W during the encounter. Retracting too much is also a mistake.
Parker Solar Probe has flown through coronal mass ejections and measured their plasma from the inside.
Turning to transmit takes the radiators out of the shield's shadow: close to the Sun, heat rises within minutes.
source: Landis et al., AIAA 2008-5712, p. 7 (radiators behind the shield)

text: Parker stores its perihelion data and sends it to Earth once it moves away from the Sun.
The paper ruled out the Stirling converter for lack of flight heritage, even though its efficiency was good.
⚗ The module ejection and the return capsule are game fiction: Parker does not return to Earth.
Only ~10 h of each pass is spent within 10 solar radii. That is the core of the mission.
